surveyDefinition.title: Electric Vehicles — consumer survey (Global)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on their EV purchase journey, charging and range requirements, and value orientation.

segments.name: Value-Optimizing Buyers
segments.description: Highly price-sensitive, compare total cost of ownership against gas vehicles, seek incentives and low running costs, willing to compromise on range or features for a lower price.

segments.name: Range-Prioritizing Buyers
segments.description: Need maximum range and reliable charging for long commutes or rural driving, less price-sensitive if range needs are met, will reject EVs that cannot cover their typical trips.

segments.name: Convenience-Seeking Buyers
segments.description: Value seamless charging at home or work, prefer EVs that integrate into their daily routine with minimal effort, moderate price sensitivity, prioritize ease of ownership.

segments.name: Lifestyle-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Motivated by environmental values, technology, or status, less price-sensitive, willing to pay a premium for the latest features, brand image, or sustainability credentials.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Electric Vehicles buyers worldwide. It asks how people use Electric Vehicles, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories. This global view is not a separate fieldwork exercise: it selects the strongest questions from the regional surveys and blends their percentages using population-style regional weights.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults worldwide who buy or use Electric Vehicles for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Adults aged 18+ who are the primary decision-maker or co-decision-maker for a household vehicle purchase; Currently own or lease a vehicle, or intend to purchase/lease one within the next 24 months; Have a valid driver's license; Household income sufficient to afford a new EV (or used EV) in their market. Excluded: Fleet managers or business purchasers buying EVs for commercial use; Individuals without a driver's license or no intention to purchase a vehicle; Residents of areas with no EV charging infrastructure and no plans to install home charging.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Individual consumers buy and pay for electric vehicles for personal use, and they make the purchase decision (often with input from household members). While businesses also purchase EVs for fleets, the primary consumer market is substantial and well-defined.
respondentBehaviours: Actively considering or planning to purchase a new vehicle within the next 12-24 months
Researching vehicle options online, comparing models, reading reviews
Value fuel savings, lower maintenance, and environmental benefits
May have test-driven an EV or visited a dealership
Consider charging convenience and range as key decision factors
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: EV Ownership & Usage Context
sections.covers: Establishes the respondent's current relationship with EVs (owner, considerer, rejecter), their driving habits, and the role of the vehicle in their household.

sections.label: EV Purchase Journey & Decision Drivers
sections.covers: Explores what triggers EV consideration, how respondents research and compare options, where they would buy, and the key factors that drive or block the purchase decision.

sections.label: EV Requirements & Trade-offs
sections.covers: Identifies the non-negotiable attributes of an EV (range, charging speed, price), the quality cues that matter, and the trade-offs buyers are willing to make.

sections.label: Satisfaction, Loyalty & Future Intent
sections.covers: Measures satisfaction with current EV ownership or the consideration process, identifies friction points, and gauges likelihood to recommend and future adoption plans.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey begins by understanding the respondent's current driving context and where they are in the EV consideration journey. It then walks through the purchase journey, from triggers and research to budget and decision factors. Next, it explores the specific requirements and trade-offs around range, charging, and value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, friction, and future adoption intent, allowing us to segment respondents by their value orientation and charging/range needs.

questions.insight: Top response: We are actively considering buying an EV (41.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Lifestyle-Driven and Convenience-Seeking Buyers drive ownership, while Value-Optimizing and Range-Prioritizing Buyers are still in the consideration phase.

questions.question: How many electric vehicles does your household currently own or lease?
questions.insight: Top response: 1 (82.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Most EV-owning households have a single EV, typical of Convenience-Seeking and Value-Optimizing Buyers who use it as a primary or secondary vehicle.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the electric vehicle in your household?
options: Daily commute to work or school

data.label: Daily commute to work or school

questions.insight: Top response: Daily commute to work or school (52.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Daily commuting is the dominant use case, driven by Convenience-Seeking and Value-Optimizing Buyers; Range-Prioritizing Buyers account for the long-distance share.

questions.question: What is the main reason you use an electric vehicle for most of your trips?
options: Access to carpool lanes or parking perks
It's the only car we have

data.label: Access to carpool lanes or parking perks
It's the only car we have

questions.insight: Top response: Lower running costs than gas (44.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Cost savings are the primary driver for Value-Optimizing Buyers, while Lifestyle-Driven Buyers split between environmental and technology motivations.

questions.question: In a typical week, how many days do you drive the electric vehicle?
questions.insight: Top response: 5-6 days (35.00%).
questions.distributionNote: EVs are used frequently, with Convenience-Seeking and Value-Optimizing Buyers relying on them for daily commutes.

questions.question: How often do you drive your electric vehicle on a trip longer than 150 miles one way?
questions.insight: Top response: A few times a year (40.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Long trips are occasional for most, but Range-Prioritizing Buyers take them more frequently, while Convenience-Seeking Buyers avoid them when possible.

questions.question: Who in your household makes the final decision on which car to buy?
questions.insight: Top response: I do (45.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Decisions are largely individual or joint, reflecting the diverse household structures across all buyer segments.

questions.question: How long did you research before buying your most recent electric vehicle?
questions.insight: Top response: 1 to 3 months (34.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Value-Optimizing Buyers and Range-Prioritizing Buyers dominate, leading to a moderate research period as they compare costs and range; Lifestyle-Driven Buyers extend the tail with longer research for premium features.

questions.question: Where did you first learn about the electric vehicle you bought?
questions.insight: Top response: Online search or comparison websites (34.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Value-Optimizing and Range-Prioritizing Buyers start with online research; Convenience-Seeking Buyers may discover through dealerships; Lifestyle-Driven Buyers are influenced by news and reviews.

questions.insight: Top response: Brand dealership (new) (62.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Convenience-Seeking and Lifestyle-Driven Buyers prefer traditional dealerships for seamless service; Value-Optimizing Buyers explore used and online channels for affordability.

questions.question: What is the highest price you are considering paying for your next electric vehicle?
questions.distributionNote: Value-Optimizing Buyers concentrate in the lower brackets; Range-Prioritizing Buyers spread across mid-to-high for adequate range; Lifestyle-Driven Buyers pull the premium end.

questions.question: Which factors most influenced your final choice of electric vehicle?

questions.question: What is the minimum driving range you would accept for your next electric vehicle?
questions.insight: Top response: 300 miles or more (30.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Range-Prioritizing Buyers and Value-Optimizing Buyers split the middle; a substantial share of Range-Prioritizing Buyers demands 300+ miles, while Value-Optimizing Buyers accept lower ranges for affordability.

metadata.storyline_summary: The survey begins by understanding the respondent's current driving context and where they are in the EV consideration journey. It then walks through the purchase journey, from triggers and research to budget and decision factors. Next, it explores the specific requirements and trade-offs around range, charging, and value. Finally, it measures satisfaction, friction, and future adoption intent, allowing us to segment respondents by their value orientation and charging/range needs.
metadata.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on their EV purchase journey, charging and range requirements, and value orientation.
metadata.segmentation_lens: Price sensitivity / value orientation combined with usage/behavioural (charging and range needs). This lens separates buyers because the high upfront premium and ongoing charging costs create distinct value-driven trade-offs that directly shape purchase behaviour, more than usage frequency alone.

segments.name: Value-Optimizing Buyers
segments.description: Highly price-sensitive, compare total cost of ownership against gas vehicles, seek incentives and low running costs, willing to compromise on range or features for a lower price.
segments.hypothesis: They will prioritize price and incentives over brand or performance, and will be more likely to consider used EVs or smaller battery options.

segments.name: Range-Prioritizing Buyers
segments.description: Need maximum range and reliable charging for long commutes or rural driving, less price-sensitive if range needs are met, will reject EVs that cannot cover their typical trips.
segments.hypothesis: They will rank range and charging speed as non-negotiable, and will be more likely to consider premium or long-range models despite higher cost.

segments.name: Convenience-Seeking Buyers
segments.description: Value seamless charging at home or work, prefer EVs that integrate into their daily routine with minimal effort, moderate price sensitivity, prioritize ease of ownership.
segments.hypothesis: They will prioritize home charging access and charging network reliability over raw range, and will be less willing to tolerate public charging inconvenience.

segments.name: Lifestyle-Driven Buyers
segments.description: Motivated by environmental values, technology, or status, less price-sensitive, willing to pay a premium for the latest features, brand image, or sustainability credentials.
segments.hypothesis: They will prioritize brand, technology, and environmental impact over cost, and will be more likely to consider luxury or early-adopter models.

segmentModel.tie_break: Question bb8 (most influential factor in final choice) is the most direct behavioural self-report because it forces respondents to pick the single factor that actually drove their purchase decision, cleanly separating range, price, technology, and environmental motives.
notes: Convenience seekers are primarily identified by home charging preference and daily commute use; they have fewer explicit signals because the survey focuses more on range and value.
Lifestyle drivers are identified by environmental/tech motivations and willingness to pay premium.
Value optimizers are identified by price sensitivity and cost-related motivations.
Range prioritizers are identified by long-distance needs and high range requirements.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.
